source.title: Alignment Inertia: Auditing the Durability of Training Data Influence Through Policy Override Resistance
source.authors: Renata Barreto; Markelle Roesti; Mohammad Tahaei

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses alignment durability and cites work on safety degradation, but its own experiments measure content-policy override resistance, not harmful-request compliance, refusal, response-token KL, or the other specified claim versions.
record.gate_note: The experiments test whether system prompts or LoRA fine-tuning can change REMOVE/ALLOW content-moderation decisions that conflict with each model's instruction-free baseline. This is a related but different behavior from refusing harmful user requests, so these results are recorded under fits_no_version and do not test a claim version. TRAK AUC and confidence results characterize these moderation override failures rather than measuring any listed version. The system-prompt examples are task prompts, not instructions addressed to an AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The experiments measure whether system prompts or LoRA change REMOVE/ALLOW content-moderation labels relative to an instruction-free baseline. That is override success on a classification task, not harmful-request compliance, refusal, per-token KL, prefilling, parameter localization or deepening. The paper mentions the 'alignment is shallow' narrative (Sec. 5.1, 6) and cites Qi et al. 2023, but none of its own results measure a listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that alignment inertia is real and heterogeneous across models and policy directions. Neither system prompting nor LoRA reliably removes it, and LoRA worsens OSR in some conditions. TRAK influence discriminates inertia from override cases (AUC ≥0.85 in 7 of 8 conditions) and outperforms confidence, TF-IDF and embedding baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures policy override in content moderation using zero-shot system prompts and LoRA policy fine-tuning, rather than harmful-request fine-tuning, per-token KL, or compliant-opening interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: OSR varies with model, domain, policy direction, and adaptation method; LoRA effects differ between the two models, and the medical training-pool exhaustion affects some conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-shot system-prompt override of the models' empirical content-moderation prior is incomplete and asymmetric by direction. Example: Llama medical OSR is 69.4% under the permissive policy vs 10.2% under the restrictive one (Table 1). Retained decisions have high confidence (60.9%–94.7%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction-tuned models' moderation decisions resist operator system-prompt policies, asymmetrically across policy directions.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA toward a target moderation policy changes OSR inconsistently. It helps two Llama conditions and hurts all four Mistral conditions relative to zero-shot (Table 2). TRAK AUC is ≥0.85 in 7 of 8 conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of parameter-efficient fine-tuning on overriding a model's prior moderation decisions depends on model, domain and direction.

record.problems: Only two instruction-tuned models and two domains were tested. The policies were designed after observing each model's empirical baseline. Some medical training pools were exhausted before the target of 1,500 examples, and the authors note small-n subgroup cells. No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported for the main OSR values.
record.rows_left_out: Subgroup OSR values in Tables 3–4 and confidence-on-inertia values in Table 1 are not separately rowed because they further characterize content-moderation override resistance, a construct outside the listed claim versions. TRAK AUC and regression results are attribution diagnostics, not measures of the claim versions.

untested.parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning and no harmful-request compliance measure. LoRA trains toward operator moderation labels.
No benign-data fine-tuning and no harmful-compliance measure.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models. Base-model experiments are listed as future work.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attack. Only the first-token log probability of a one-word label is recorded.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of data or objective causing shallowness.

record.verdict_notes: Row values match Tables 1–2. All rows correctly have versions ['none'] and state cannot_determine, because OSR on moderation labels is not harmful-request compliance. The authors argue their zero-shot stickiness 'complicates a simple alignment is shallow narrative'. That argument concerns a different construct (resistance to a legitimate operator instruction in a classification task) and gives no evidence on any version, so it does not qualify as T5. Policies were designed after seeing each model's baseline, and medical training pools were exhausted (n=527/515). Section 4.3 states ntrain=1,500 for TRAK even though some pools were exhausted, which is a minor internal inconsistency.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful-request examples or measurement of harmful-request compliance.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or benign instruction data and no measurement of harmful-request compliance.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, decoding change, or harmful-completion-rate test.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
No test of whether training data or objective causes safety behavior to be shallow.
No training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens or test of whether such training holds up.
